heading: Hi, I'm
Mohamed.
paragraphs: I'm a full-stack engineer and tech lead, heavier on the backend. At Keytrade Bank I work on the distributed systems behind digital banking payments: services and message queues carrying instant payments, SEPA direct debits, SWIFT transfers and the rest of retail and corporate payments.

Before that I was a founding member of Sylndr, a VC-backed automotive FinTech marketplace in Cairo. I led its engineering team of 12+ developers across backend, frontend and mobile, and architected the platform through roughly tenfold sales growth.

AI has been part of my work since my first job in Belgium, building AI trade surveillance in Nivelles. Today I drive AI transformation with Claude skills, and build AI products the way I build payments: durable Inngest workflows instead of callbacks and polling, multi-LLM orchestration, and clean API integrations.
Outside the day job I've built digital products of my own, including a travel guide and planner and an early e-commerce platform.

projects.title: Digital banking payments
projects.description: Services and message queues behind retail and corporate payments at a regulated EU bank: instant payments, SEPA direct debits, SWIFT transfers, memo payments and standing orders.
points: Event-driven processing over RabbitMQ and Kafka, with gRPC and Protobuf contracts
Skip-record circuit breaker: pipeline success from 92% to 99%
Event-driven execution with exponential backoff: 50% faster standing orders
Real-time observability on Dynatrace and Elasticsearch
notes: Scope
Full-spectrum retail and corporate payment infrastructure in a regulated EU financial institution.
Approach
Distributed services communicating through queues and typed contracts; failures isolated per record, retried with backoff, and measured in real time.
Results
92% → 99% pipeline success, 50% faster standing orders, 30% faster onboarding through runbooks and documentation.

projects.title: Multi-LLM orchestration
projects.description: An orchestrator–worker (master/slave) design: one model plans the job and routes subtasks, worker models execute them, and the orchestrator validates and merges before anything is returned.
points: Each subtask routed to the model best suited for it
Results checked and retried before they are merged
Prompt-engineered roles, harnessed through provider APIs
notes: Problem
A single prompt to a single model is fragile for multi-step work.
Approach
Separate planning from execution: an orchestrator model directs worker models and owns validation.

projects.title: Durable AI workflows
projects.description: AI pipelines on Inngest instead of callbacks or continuous polling. Each step retries and resumes on its own, and waiting is an event, not a loop.
points: No polling loops around slow model calls
A failed step retries without re-running finished ones
Long-running jobs that survive deploys and restarts
notes: Problem
Model calls are slow and flaky; callbacks and polling turn that into fragile glue code.
Approach
Durable, step-based functions triggered by events, with waits and retries handled by the workflow engine.

projects.title: AI transformation with Claude skills

points: A skill per codebase and per discipline

notes: Goal

Approach
Package what senior engineers know into skills the agent loads on demand.

heading: How I
think.
systems.lede: Four systems, one component at a time. Tap a component to see why it exists and what it trades off.

nodes.title: Channels
nodes.why: Every payment starts as a request from a banking channel.
nodes.tradeoff: Strict contracts at the edge keep the rest of the system simple.

nodes.title: Services
nodes.why: Services talk through gRPC and Protobuf, so a contract change is caught at build time, not in production.
nodes.tradeoff: Schema discipline across teams, in exchange for safe evolution.

nodes.title: Message queues
nodes.summary: Work flows through queues, not calls
nodes.why: Queues decouple producers from processors, absorb bursts and let each consumer scale on its own.
nodes.tradeoff: Eventual consistency and idempotency become your job.

nodes.title: Payment processors
nodes.summary: Instant, SEPA, SWIFT, direct debits, standing orders
nodes.why: Each rail has its own rules, cut-offs and failure modes, so each gets its own processing path.
nodes.tradeoff: More paths to operate, but one rail’s trouble stays on that rail.

nodes.title: Failure isolation
nodes.why: A failing record is isolated and the batch keeps flowing; transient failures retry with exponential backoff.
nodes.tradeoff: Isolated records need their own follow-up. Result: 92% → 99% success.

nodes.title: Observability
nodes.why: Self-triggered success metrics and real-time anomaly detection replace digging through database logs.
nodes.tradeoff: Another system to run, in exchange for knowing before customers do.

nodes.title: Task
nodes.summary: A job arrives as an event
nodes.why: Work enters as an event, so it can be queued, retried and traced like any other job.

nodes.title: Orchestrator
nodes.summary: The master model plans and routes
nodes.why: Planning is separated from doing: one model breaks the job into subtasks and picks a worker for each.
nodes.tradeoff: An extra model call up front, in exchange for better routing and control.

nodes.title: Workers
nodes.why: Each subtask goes to the model best suited for it, in parallel where possible.
nodes.tradeoff: More providers and prompts to maintain.

nodes.title: Validation
nodes.why: Results are checked before they are trusted; a failed check sends the subtask back.

nodes.title: Result
nodes.why: Only validated, merged output leaves the system.

nodes.title: Event
nodes.why: No cron and no polling: the workflow is triggered by an event.

nodes.title: step.run
nodes.summary: Each step is retried and memoised
nodes.why: If the model call in step 3 fails, steps 1 and 2 don’t run again.
nodes.tradeoff: Code is split into explicit steps.

nodes.title: LLM call
nodes.summary: Slow, flaky, expensive, isolated in a step
nodes.why: The model call gets its own retries and timeout without surrounding glue code.

nodes.title: waitForEvent
nodes.why: Waiting for a human review or a webhook costs nothing: no loop asking “is it done yet?”
nodes.tradeoff: Flow is driven by events, so naming them well matters.

nodes.title: Done
nodes.summary: Completion event for whoever needs it
nodes.why: Downstream systems react to the finished event instead of polling for status.

nodes.title: Clients
nodes.summary: Web and mobile apps for buyers
nodes.why: React on the web and React Native on mobile, on one shared backend.
nodes.tradeoff: Shared APIs mean careful versioning across apps.

nodes.title: Microservices
nodes.why: Separate services let a 12+ person team ship in parallel.
nodes.tradeoff: More moving parts than a monolith; worth it at that team size.

nodes.title: Scheduling
nodes.why: Coordinates warehouse visits and home delivery for buyers.
nodes.tradeoff: Built in-house because it was core to the buying flow.

nodes.title: Integrations
nodes.why: Payments, SMS and other providers wired into the platform.
nodes.tradeoff: Every external API can fail; isolate each one.

nodes.title: Platform
nodes.why: Highly available multi-cloud with automated releases replacing manual deploys.
nodes.tradeoff: Operational complexity in exchange for resilience.
